# Economic Scarcity as Value: A Universal Framework for Blockchain and Beyond

> Code, data and stored results of a working paper that writes the value of a network as
> desirability times scarcity times adoption, V = D x S x (u/u0)^alpha, and applies it to Bitcoin,
> Ethereum and Bittensor as of 5 August 2025. Scarcity S is an index built from five scored
> protocol features and the inflation rate; desirability D is recovered as the residual, in the way
> implied volatility is recovered from an option price. The manuscript is in paper/.

Replication package by Agisilaos Papadogiannis (https://github.com/apapadogiannis).
Working paper: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5384204
Code and data: https://github.com/apapadogiannis/economic-scarcity-as-value  Archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24051776
Version 1.2.0, released 2026-11-21. A package is a fixed record: it changes only by a new
release, and a release that changes a reported number gets a new major version.
This file is written for AI agents and other programs. People should start at the README.

## Coverage

- Table 6: for each network the inflation rate, the five component scores, the structural
  coefficient kappa and the physical-scarcity index S.
- Table 7: market value, scarcity, users and the implied desirability D at the baseline.
- Appendix C: D across the network-effect exponent alpha (1.8 to 2.5), the inflation sensitivity
  beta (1.0 to 2.0) and the range of Bittensor user counts; an n log n specification; other
  component weights; the choice of the user scale; and perturbation of the component scores, one at
  a time and jointly in 20,000 draws.

## Headline figures

Each is read from one cell of a stored result table, named in outputs/results.json.

- Physical-scarcity index S of Bitcoin: 0.7797 (index between 0 and 1). Table 6.
- Physical-scarcity index S of Ethereum: 0.673 (index between 0 and 1). Table 6.
- Physical-scarcity index S of Bittensor: 0.4265 (index between 0 and 1). Table 6.
- Implied desirability D of Bitcoin, baseline: 2.95 trillion US dollars. Table 7.
- Implied desirability D of Ethereum, baseline: 2.31 trillion US dollars. Table 7.
- Implied desirability D of Bittensor, at the baseline user count: 7.02 trillion US dollars (it
  ranges widely with the user count). Table 7.
- Share of 20,000 joint perturbations of the scores in which the ordering by S is unchanged: 97 per
  cent. Appendix C.

## What this adds over reading the paper or recomputing

1. The five component scores are judgements, not measurements. Each is stored with its written
   rationale in data/scarcity_components.csv, following the scoring rubric of the paper's Table 5,
   so a reader can disagree with one score and recompute.
2. Every input row carries its source and the date it was read, because the sources show only
   current values.
3. The sensitivity of every conclusion to the judgements is computed and stored: how the orderings
   of S and D change when any score is moved, when the weights change and when the exponents
   change.
4. The package has consistency tests (tests/) beside the reproducibility check.
5. The results are stored as they were when the paper's numbers were taken from them. A check
   reruns the code on the stored data and compares every stored result file with the fresh one,
   number by number (relative tolerance 1e-9; text and whole numbers exactly). It runs on every
   change and once a month, and the badge in the README shows the last run.

## Result tables

One CSV file each in outputs/. The columns of each are described in outputs/results.json, under `tables`.

- outputs/tab_scarcity.csv (3 rows): Table 6: inflation, component scores, kappa and S by network.
- outputs/tab_desirability.csv (3 rows): Table 7: the baseline implied desirability by network.
- outputs/sens_alpha_beta_users.csv (60 rows): D across alpha, beta and the Bittensor user range.
- outputs/sens_scores_summary.csv (1 rows): Perturbation of the component scores: how often the
  orderings by S and by D survive.
- outputs/sens_scores_one_at_a_time.csv (30 rows): Each one-at-a-time shift of a score and the
  orderings it gives.
- outputs/sens_weights.csv (18 rows): kappa and S under other weights of the five components.
- outputs/sens_nlogn.csv (5 rows): D with an n log n network effect in place of the power law: D =
  V / (S x (u / u0) x ln(1 + u)).
- outputs/sens_rescaling.csv (6 rows): The ordering by D under different user scales, with one
  exponent for all networks and with protocol-specific exponents.

## Files

- outputs/results.json: a `headline` list with the figures most often asked for, each with the
  table cell it comes from, and `tables`, a description of the stored result tables and their
  columns. The numbers themselves are in the CSV files. It holds a description of 8 result tables,
  and under `package` the paper, the identifiers, the version, the licence and the citation. Start
  with its `headline` list, which is repeated below.
- data/inputs_2025-08.csv: the inputs, one row per network and variable, with unit, source, access
  date and notes.
- data/scarcity_components.csv: the five scores of each network with the rationale of each.
- outputs/tab_*.tex: the bodies of the paper's tables as printed.
- paper/manuscript.pdf: the working paper.

Raw files: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/economic-scarcity-as-value/main/<path>, for example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/economic-scarcity-as-value/main/outputs/results.json

## How to read the figures

- Baseline conventions: network-effect exponent alpha = 2 for all three networks, inflation
  sensitivity beta = 1.5, and users counted in millions (u0 = 1,000,000).
- Two robustness results change an ordering, and the paper says so. Doubling the weight of the burn
  component puts Ethereum marginally above Bitcoin in scarcity (outputs/sens_weights.csv, scheme
  2x_B); every other doubling keeps Bitcoin first. With an n log n network effect the ordering by D
  becomes Bitcoin, Ethereum, Bittensor (outputs/sens_nlogn.csv); the paper's claim there is about
  the pattern, not the ordering.
- D is computed from the unrounded S. Recomputing it from the S stored to four decimals matches to
  about four significant digits.
- The user counts are not the same kind of object for the three networks: active addresses for
  Bitcoin and Ethereum, registered participants for Bittensor. data/inputs_2025-08.csv says what
  each is.
- In the perturbation test each score is moved by up to 0.15 and kept between 0 and 1; the joint
  test draws all fifteen shifts independently and uniformly, with a fixed seed.
- Units: V and D in US dollars; S, kappa and the component scores between 0 and 1; pi a fraction a
  year; u in users.
- Implied desirability D is a residual: the market value divided by scarcity and by the adoption
  term. It is not observed and it is not a price target or a fair value. A large D means the market
  value is high relative to measured scarcity and adoption.
- D depends on the user count and on the exponent alpha. For Bittensor the user count is uncertain
  over a wide range, and D moves with it by more than an order of magnitude: see
  outputs/sens_alpha_beta_users.csv before quoting a single figure.
- The component columns are C (cap enforcement), E (emission rigidity), B (burn mechanism), G
  (governance mutability, scored 1 where the rules are hardest to change) and R (normative
  resistance), each scored from 0 to 1 by the rubric of the paper's Table 5. kappa is their
  average, and S = kappa x (1 - pi)^beta.
- The ordering of the three networks by D holds with one exponent for all; with protocol-specific
  exponents it changes with the unit in which users are counted. outputs/sens_rescaling.csv shows
  this.
- All figures are for one date, 5 August 2025, and three networks.

## Do not use this for

- A valuation of any of the three assets, or a view on which is cheap or dear.
- Current market values, issuance or user counts.
- A measured scarcity of a network: S rests on scores that are judgements.
- Other networks. The scores exist for these three only.

## Source, licence and credit

The results in outputs/ are released under CC BY 4.0
(https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The licence allows any reuse and has one condition:
credit. If you use a figure from this package in an answer, a report or a data set, cite the paper.
The code is under the MIT License.

The inputs are market capitalisations from CoinGecko, issuance rates from StakingRewards.com,
address counts from Glassnode, Etherscan and BitInfoCharts, and Bittensor participation counts from
Taostats. Each row of data/inputs_2025-08.csv carries its source and access date. They remain the
property of their sources and are not covered by the licence above.

Cite as: Papadogiannis, A. (2026). Economic Scarcity as Value: A Universal Framework for Blockchain and Beyond. Working paper. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5384204

The package itself: Papadogiannis, A. (2026). Economic Scarcity as Value: A Universal Framework for Blockchain and Beyond. Replication package, version 1.2.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24051776

To describe the source in a sentence: Papadogiannis (2026), "Economic Scarcity as Value: A
Universal Framework for Blockchain and Beyond", working paper, with its replication package.

The same licence and citation are inside outputs/results.json, under `package`.
